newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 25.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Friday:
* The U.S. Justice Department announced it would not try to block the $22-billion-merger of Bell Atlantic and NYNEX, after a nine-month investigation.
* Troubled upscale clothing retailer Barney's said that in February, Saks Holdings made a $330-million-offer for the company that it rejected as too low.
* Hints of possible further interest-rate increases, including comments by Fed governor Laurence Meyer, caused Treasury prices to decline.
* Procter & Gamble posted a 16-percent gain in quarterly earnings, boosted by cost-cutting efforts.
* American Express quarterly earnings increased about 15 percent due to more business in its credit and charge cards and mutual fund sales.
* The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 20.47 points at 6,792.25, as rate worries won out over a technology rally.
* Airlines Delta and Southwest posted strong profits even though fuel costs rose. Southwest shares rose but Delta stock fell.
* MCI Communications first quarter profits were unchanged as higher long-distance profits were offset by losses from new wireless and local phone businesses.
* Kidder, Peabody agreed to pay $14.1 million to settle a class-action suit accusing it and other firms of fixing prices on the Nasdaq stock market.
* In exchange for tax incentives and energy discounts, Standard & Poor's agreed to stay in New York City through the year 2019.

* House Banking Committee Chairman Jim Leach asked the Clinton Administration to review the expansion plans and investments of The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp, Fannie Mae and the Federal Home Loan Bank System.
* The new U.S. economic sanctions on Burma have resonated throughout the region.
* Market place: "Best execution", or getting customers the lowest available price when they buy stock and the highest when they sell, is not as simple as it sounds.
* Auto makers have decided that Brazil and Argentina could be an even more profitable market than southeast Asia or Eastern Europe.
